title: Your Nitnem, chosen
hookLine: write down the daily prayer you will keep
tomorrow: no gurdwara near campus. so where does Simran's seva go?

lines: A DORM, A ROOMMATE, AN EARLY CLASS.
ALL OF THEM, OR WHAT YOU'LL KEEP?
cards: The housing email lands at dinner: a dorm room, a roommate from another state, and an eight o'clock class. No Bebe across the yard. No chili rows at dawn.
Simran reads it out, then asks the question everyone at the table has been waiting for. Which prayers come with me? Bebe answers first: all of them, the whole Nitnem, every day.
Her dad puts down his fork. Start with what you'll actually keep.

teach.h: ANG 305: RISE EARLY, KEEP THE NAME.
teach.b: Nitnem is the daily rule of prayer. Guru Ram Das paints the picture on Ang 305, paraphrased: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early and keeps the Name in mind.
The Sikh code, the Rehat Maryada, names the banis: the Japji, the Jaap and others at dawn, Rehras in the evening, Sohila at night. Some families and groups add more.
So here are the two views at Simran's table, and both are real. Bebe's: a rule is a rule because it doesn't bend to your mood.

teach.h: KEEP IT WHOLE, WHATEVER THE MOOD.
teach.b: Keep the Nitnem whole, on tired days and busy ones, and the keeping becomes the practice. If you trim it whenever life gets loud, life will always be loud.
Harjit's: a rule you break by week two teaches you that you break rules.

teach.h: KEEP WHAT YOU CAN, AND GROW.
teach.b: Start with what you can keep every single day, the Japji at dawn and Sohila at night, and grow toward the whole. Bebe says that's how habits shrink. Harjit says that's how they last.
Simran listens to both of them for a long time.
Then she gets a pen and a sticky note, and writes the first line of her Nitnem, the one she'll keep in a dorm with a sleeping roommate.

how: Sikhs keep Nitnem by reciting set banis each day, the Japji and others in the morning, Rehras in the evening and Sohila at night, often from a gutka; some recite from memory, some listen to recordings, and some families and groups include more banis.

o: the daily prayers you choose to keep, written down
a yearly vow renewed each Vaisakhi at the gurdwara
a prayer said only before a long journey

games.q: the Nitnem table — tap the pairs.
p: a Sikh rises early for the Name
keep it whole, whatever the mood
keep what you can, and grow

s: Nitnem means praying whenever you happen to feel like it
it's a daily rule: set banis at dawn, in the evening and at night.
Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh rising early to keep the Name
Ang 305, paraphrased: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early.
every Sikh family recites exactly the same set of banis
the code names the banis, and some families and groups add more.

games.q: you lean toward starting small. a friend asks you to give the best case for keeping the full Nitnem from day one. what do you say?
o: a rule that never bends to your mood trains you; keeping it whole is the practice.
the full Nitnem earns more blessing per minute than a short prayer ever could.
a shorter Nitnem doesn't count at all, so there's no point starting with one.
games.why: the strongest case for the whole Nitnem is about steadiness: a rule kept on tired and busy days becomes the practice. the other two are not what either side says.

practice: On paper, write the daily prayer you'll keep: which bani, what time, where you'll be. Make it something you could keep on your worst day, and if you're aiming for more, write that underneath. Read it back to yourself once, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Your Nitnem: the daily rule of prayer, chosen by you and written down, whole or growing toward whole.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the daily rule, a Sikh's set prayers for each day.

carryVoice: Pocket this: my nitnem, written down where I'll see it at dawn. One sticky note, already on the mirror.
